N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) is a probable human carcinogen found in contaminated pharmaceuticals and drinking water, yet the impact of age on NDMA susceptibility remains poorly understood. Using DNA repair-deﬁcient (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) and wild-type mice, we systematically compare the effects of NDMA exposure in juveniles and adults. Juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice are profoundly more vulnerable, exhibiting persistent DNA damage, inﬂammation, and mutations that lead to liver pathology and tumorigenesis, particularly in males. Adults, by comparison, are resistant to NDMA. Wild-type mice show similar, attenuated trends. NDMA-induced DNA adduct levels are comparable across age groups, implicating proliferation-dependent responses to adducts, rather than adduct formation, as the primary driver of age-related risk. Supporting this mechanism, triiodothyronine-stimulated cell proliferation in adults partially recapitulates juvenile sensitivity, linking cell division to NDMA genotoxicity. Our ﬁndings identify developmental stage, sex, and DNA repair capacity as key modiﬁers of NDMA-induced carcinogenesis, with potential implications for environmental risk assessment and regulatory policy.

While children and adolescents account for a quarter of the population, our understanding of their potential heightened risk from environmental carcinogens remains limited1. In this study, we investigated the role of age as a susceptibility factor to N-nitrosamine exposure. N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), a probable human carcinogen, exempliﬁes this concern2. NDMA has been detected in various sources,

including food, drinking water, cigarette smoke, and pharmaceuticals. Although epidemiological evidence in humans remains limited, there are studies that link NDMA exposure to elevated risks of bladder, stomach, prostate, and liver cancers, as well as leukemia and multiple myeloma2,3. Understanding the mechanisms underlying age-dependent responses to NDMA in experimental models is therefore critical. NDMA exposure through inhalation, ingestion, or injection increases the incidence of liver, lung, and kidney tumors in rodents2. The adverse health effects of NDMA exposure in animals are most severe in the liver and include centrilobular necrosis, hemorrhage, ﬁbrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and cancer. NDMA’s mutagenicity arises from its metabolism by cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1), which generates the highly reactive methyldiazonium ion. This intermediate methylates DNA to form mutagenic adducts such as O6- methylguanine (O6MeG) and 3-methyladenine (3MeA). If unrepaired, these adducts can induce mutations, toxicity, and inﬂammation, thus promoting carcinogenesis and aging2,4–10. O6MeG is restored to guanine through direct reversal by the suicide protein O6-methylguanine- DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), while the remediation of 3MeA via base excision repair is initiated by 3-alkyladenine DNA glycosylase (AAG/MPG). Mice lacking MGMT or AAG exhibit heightened susceptibility to NDMA-induced genotoxicity and tumorigenesis2,4–10. In MGMT knockout mice, O6MeG mispairs with thymine during replication, while in AAG knockouts, 3MeA is bypassed with errors, both increasing point mutations4–10. Mismatch repair of O6MeG/T can generate singlestranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps and double-strand breaks (DSBs), and replication-blocking adducts like 3MeA can lead to replication fork stress4,5,7–12. These lesions may be resolved via homologous recombination, which can cause large-scale sequence rearrangements including deletions, translocations, or loss of heterozygosity, all of which are commonly associated with cancer4,7. Collectively, these mechanisms illustrate the mutagenic potential of unrepaired NDMA-induced adducts. The downstream consequences of NDMA-induced DNA adduct formation extend beyond mutagenesis. Persistent mismatches, ssDNA gaps, stalled forks, and DSBs activate DNA damage response (DDR) pathways, triggering both cell death and compensatory tissue regeneration11–15. These DDR pathways concurrently stimulate inﬂammatory responses and interferon signaling, driving the activation of hepatic progenitor cells and resident macrophages, as well as the recruitment of circulating immune cells to injury sites. While these processes initially function to promote repair, chronic activation fosters tumorigenesis by enhancing cellular proliferation and survival signaling, thus creating a microenvironment conducive to mutation accumulation14–17. Although NDMA toxicity has been widely studied in animal models, the inﬂuence of age on the severity of NDMA-induced DNA damage, inﬂammation, mutagenesis, and long-term liver pathology remains largely unexplored2. To address this knowledge gap, we exposed both juvenile and adult mice to NDMA via drinking water and systematically evaluated molecular, cellular, and tissue-level responses. We utilized mice lacking both AAG and MGMT genes (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) as a mechanistic model that serves several critical purposes: (1) both MGMT and AAG exhibit substantial interindividual variation in humans2,4,7, making the model relevant to studies of geneenvironment interactions; (2) the model ampliﬁes NDMA-induced responses, thus requiring fewer animals; and (3) it provides mechanistic insights into how DNA repair capacity and age interact to inﬂuence carcinogenic outcomes. We selected a relatively high drinking water dose of 5 ppm NDMA to ensure measurable biological effects within the two-week exposure period and to align with established toxicological studies2. Using this approach, we show that age is a critical determinant of the NDMA response, with younger mice exhibiting substantially greater DNA damage, interferon-mediated inﬂammation, mutations, and liver pathology. While this age-dependent susceptibility was most

pronounced in DNA repair-deﬁcient mice, a similar effect was also observed in WT animals, demonstrating developmental stage as a key risk factor even when repair pathways are intact. Importantly, neither CYP2E1 expression nor DNA adduct levels varied signiﬁcantly by age, suggesting that age-related risk reﬂects the proliferation-dependent processing of adducts rather than differences in metabolism. This conclusion is supported by the increased susceptibility to NDMAinduced genotoxicity in adult mice treated with proliferationstimulating triiodothyronine (T3). We also observed sex-dependent differences, consistent with known sexual dimorphism in liver biology. By revealing how age, DNA repair capacity, and sex interact to shape the response to a relevant environmental carcinogen, our study provides new insight into the mechanisms underlying early life vulnerability and highlights the importance of considering developmental stage in toxicological assessment.

Results Enhanced juvenile genotoxicity is independent of DNA adduct levels To investigate how age modulates the genotoxicity of NDMA, we exposed DNA repair-deﬁcient (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) mice to 5 ppm NDMA in drinking water for two weeks, starting at postnatal day 21 (juveniles) or day 90 (adults) (Fig. 1a, b). Formalin-ﬁxed liver sections were then analyzed for H2AX phosphorylated at Ser139 (γH2AX), a marker of replication stress and DNA DSBs18. Juvenile mice exhibited a striking increase in γH2AX levels immediately following the 14-day NDMA exposure period (14 + 0 d), an effect entirely absent in adults (Fig. 1c). Importantly, γH2AX persisted in juvenile livers 10 days post-exposure but remained undetectable in adults (Fig. 1d). Western blot analysis reinforced these age-speciﬁc disparities, revealing signiﬁcantly elevated γH2AX only in younger animals after NDMA treatment (Fig. 1e). To conﬁrm that this age-dependent response was independent of exposure route, we also administered NDMA via intraperitoneal injection (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Consistently, juvenile mice showed a stronger γH2AX response by both histology and western blot following direct exposure (Supplementary Fig. 1b, c). This robust, agedependent induction of γH2AX across exposure routes highlights the particular vulnerability of juvenile mice to unresolved replication stress and DSBs. Stressed replication forks and DNA strand breaks can trigger DDRs13. To further explore, we analyzed p53 phosphorylated at Ser15 (p-p53), a central effector in DDR pathways, which was signiﬁcantly increased in juveniles treated with 5 ppm NDMA but not in adults (Fig. 1e). Furthermore, NDMA exposure in younger mice resulted in increased total p53 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). p53 activation can lead to increased transcription of p21, promoting cell cycle arrest13. Western blot results showed p21 induction exclusively in juveniles (Fig. 1e). This p21-mediated cell cycle arrest in response to NDMA exposure provides extended time for DNA repair processes, such as homologous recombination. RAD51, critical for homologous recombination repair of DNA DSBs and replication fork processing, was upregulated only in juveniles (Fig. 1e)13. Collectively, these ﬁndings demonstrate that younger mice mount a heightened, age-dependent DDR to NDMA. Disparities in DDRs may stem from differences in adductlevels. To explore this, we quantiﬁed the levels of O6MeG and 3MeA by mass spectrometry. Both adducts were substantially increased in juveniles and adults after NDMA exposure (Fig. 1f), but no signiﬁcant differences were detected between age groups. This suggests that upstream processes such as NDMA metabolism and adduct formation are comparable across ages. Supporting this view, CYP2E1 protein levels were similar in untreated juvenile and adult control mice before and after the exposure timeline (Fig. 1g). Thus, the pronounced sensitivity of juveniles to NDMA-induced DDRs occurs independently of adduct levels. Having established that age strikingly inﬂuences the cellular response to NDMA-induced DNA damage, we next examined how

Prolonged inﬂammation and compensatory proliferation in juveniles DNA damage and responses activate interferon signaling and downstream immune pathways, which, under chronic conditions, can establish a self-perpetuating cycle of tissue injury14,17. As such, we assessed STAT1 phosphorylated at Tyr701 (pSTAT1), a central marker of the interferon response19. A signiﬁcant increase in pSTAT1 was

observed only in juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice exposed to NDMA (Fig. 2a), along with elevated total STAT1 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Adults, by contrast, exhibited no signiﬁcant changes in pSTAT1 or STAT1. Sustained interferon activation through STAT1 in response to DNA damage can lead to STAT3 activation (pSTAT3; Tyr705), forming a negative feedback loop that regulates inﬂammation and DDRs14,19,20. pSTAT3 was upregulated only in juvenile mice (Fig. 2a), reﬂecting unresolved inﬂammation. In line with this expectation, juvenile mice displayed moderately increased histiocytic and lymphocytic cell foci following NDMA exposure, an effect that was not as prominent in adults (Fig. 2b). Although inﬂammation in juveniles largely resolved by 10 days postexposure, a trend persisted (Supplementary Fig. 3a). To further investigate the mechanisms underlying the observed pathology, we examined molecular markers of immune cells. NDMA exposure in juvenile mice led to a signiﬁcant upregulation of immune cell markers CD3e (Fig. 2a) and CD11C (Supplementary Fig. 2a), indicating stimulation and recruitment of immune cells to the liver21. These immune responses were absent in adult mice, highlighting the unique vulnerability of younger animals. The recruitment and activation of immune cells drive the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), a response particularly evident in juveniles, as shown by the signiﬁcant upregulation of antioxidant enzyme HO-1 (Fig. 2a)22. This effect was also observed following intraperitoneal injection exclusively in juveniles, supporting the pronounced redox imbalance induced by NDMA in younger mice (Supplementary Fig. 1c). Excessive RONS levels can lead to hepatocellular degeneration, which was signiﬁcantly more severe in juveniles treated with 5 ppm NDMA than in adults, as evidenced by the distinct multifocal, centrilobular hepatocellular degeneration (Fig. 2b)16. This injury persisted at 10 days and even 3 months postexposure in juveniles (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b), indicating long-term hepatic damage in younger mice. To further dissect the consequences of NDMA-induced DNA adducts and associated inﬂammation, we analyzed markers of cell death across age groups. Western blot analysis demonstrated that a key apoptosis marker, cleaved caspase-3, was increased only in juvenile mice following NDMA exposure, but not adults (Fig. 2c)23. While single-cell necrosis was not immediately apparent (Fig. 2d), it became signiﬁcantly elevated only in juveniles by 10 days post treatment (Fig. 2e)24. These results indicate that younger mice sustain prolonged and multifaceted hepatocellular damage after NDMA exposure, with apoptosis dominating acutely and necrosis emerging during recovery. Following organ damage and inﬂammation, tissues undergo regenerative cell proliferation14–16. Liver regeneration, as measured by Ki67 staining, was heightened in juveniles (Fig. 2f)25. Western blot analysis conﬁrmed increased expression of proliferation markers MCM2 and PCNA speciﬁcally in juvenile mice (Supplementary Fig. 2a). This proliferative response remained elevated for at least 10 days postexposure (Fig. 2g), indicating ongoing regeneration in younger mice. In adults, Ki67 levels remained unchanged, emphasizing a lack of compensatory proliferation. When NDMA was administered via intraperitoneal injection, juveniles consistently exhibited cell death (cleaved caspase-3; Supplementary Fig. 1c) and proliferation (Ki67 and PCNA; Supplementary Fig. 1b, c), mirroring responses seen with drinking water exposure. These ﬁndings reveal that interferon-driven immune activation and oxidative stress promotes age-dependent liver injury and regenerative proliferation in juveniles.

Younger mice display persistent transcriptomic dysregulation The liver’s capacity for regeneration and detoxiﬁcation is governed by a complex network of DNA repair, cell cycle, and immune pathways, which is largely shaped by changes in gene expression14–16. To uncover how developmental stage shapes the hepatic response to NDMA, we analyzed the transcriptome in juvenile and adult Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice immediately after exposure and during recovery (Supplementary Data 1). Juvenile mice demonstrated an 11-fold increase in the number of signiﬁcantly upregulated or downregulated genes compared to adults (Fig. 3a), highlighting a much broader transcriptional disruption in younger animals. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of juveniles revealed clear segregation of NDMA-treated and untreated samples (Fig. 3b), with global gene expression patterns primarily deﬁned by NDMA exposure rather than sex. Even after a 10-day recovery, juveniles retained substantial gene expression changes, whereas adults exhibited only minor alterations (Fig. 3c). These ﬁndings reveal the magnitude of age-dependent transcriptomic reprogramming in response to NDMA. Consistent with protein-level data (Fig. 1e), juveniles exhibited robust upregulation of DDR genes, including Cdkn1a (p21), Ccng1, Ddit4l, and Pttg1, all persisting through the 10-day recovery (Fig. 3d)13,26–28. In contrast, adults showed induction of only Cdkn1a (p21) immediately following exposure, albeit 2-fold less than juveniles (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Data 1), with no corresponding, statistically signiﬁcant increase in protein levels (Fig. 1e). Pathway enrichment further revealed the exclusive activation of DDR-related pathways (p53, UV Response Up) in juveniles, with the p53 pathway continuing 10 days post-exposure (Fig. 3e). Adults showed no comparable pathway activation, underscoring their resilience. DDR orchestrates cell fate decisions, and in juveniles, we observed concurrent activation of mTORC1 signaling, a key regulator of growth and metabolism14, and apoptotic pathways (Fig. 3e). This simultaneous engagement of proliferative and cell death mechanisms in response to unresolved DNA damage uniquely characterizes the juvenile hepatic response, and is further supported by protein expression and histological analyses (Fig. 2c–g and Supplementary Fig. 2a). DNA damage and response pathways are well-established activators of innate immune signaling and subsequent inﬂammation17. In juveniles, NDMA exposure led to a signiﬁcant upregulation of immune modulators, including Stat1, Cd63, Iﬁ27, Igtp, Iigp1, Serpina3n, Ly6e, and Mbl2 (Fig. 3d)19,29,30. While expression of all of these immune-related genes remained elevated in juveniles for at least 10 days post-exposure, only one gene was induced at both timepoints in adults. Inﬂammatory processes are also known to transcriptionally suppress Cyp2e131, the primary enzyme mediating NDMA bioactivation, which was notably downregulated exclusively in younger mice even at 10 days post-exposure (Fig. 3d). This suppression likely reﬂects robust inﬂammation and stress signaling following NDMA exposure, consistent with established mechanisms in which activation of pathways such as NF-κB leads to decreased hepatic Cyp2e1 expression during liver injury and immune activation32. Paradoxically, NDMA exposure also suppressed several detoxiﬁcation genes (Fabp1, Cat, Hacl1, Oat) in juveniles, potentially exacerbating hepatotoxicity by impairing clearance mechanisms16,36–38. The concurrent upregulation of stress-responsive genes and downregulation of constitutive metabolic genes suggests unresolved hepatic injury, wherein protective mechanisms are engaged but normal detoxiﬁcation capacity remains compromised14–16,33–38. To determine whether these effects persist at lower exposure levels, we examined transcriptomic responses to a more environmentally relevant NDMA dose (5 ppb). Juveniles exhibited upregulation of cellular stress-related genes such as Cyb5r3, Cox8a, Fth1, Ftl1, Calr, Pdia3, and Exosc5 (Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Data 1)39–42, but lacked robust activation of detoxiﬁcation or inﬂammatory genes33,34. Altogether, these ﬁndings reveal a clear dosedependent response: higher NDMA concentrations in juveniles drive persistent DNA damage, inﬂammation, compensatory proliferation, and metabolic stress, fostering an environment permissive for mutation accumulation and tumor initiation. However, even brief juvenile exposure to as little as 5 ppb NDMA elicits detectable cellular stress responses, emphasizing the sensitivity of developing liver tissue to nitrosamines.

Age-dependent mutagenesis and clonal expansion in younger mice NDMA-induced DNA adducts can generate both point and largescale mutations, which are replication-dependent and may be inﬂuenced by age4–7. To assess age-related effects on NDMA mutagenesis in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice, we employed two complementary transgenic reporter systems: the gptΔ transgene, which detects point mutations via 6-thioguanine resistance in E. coli (Fig. 4a), and the RaDR transgene, which identiﬁes large-scale sequence rearrangements through restoration of EGFP expression following erroneous homologous recombination (Fig. 4b)5,6. These assays together enable precise discrimination between base-level mutations and extensive genomic alterations induced by NDMA, providing a comprehensive assessment of mutagenic mechanisms and their modulation by age. Replication-dependent misinsertions are well-established drivers of point mutations caused by NDMA exposure4–7. Using the gptΔ assay, we observed that juvenile mice exhibited substantially higher point mutation frequencies compared to adults when analyzed 3 months post-exposure (Fig. 4c). While adult mice showed no statistically signiﬁcant increase relative to controls, an upward trend suggested residual mutagenic activity. Given the severe mutational burden in the highly proliferative livers of younger mice, these ﬁndings support DNA replication as a central mechanism facilitating misinsertions and subsequent point mutations. Genotoxic ssDNA gaps, replication stress, and DSBs can induce large-scale mutations via misaligned homologous recombination events, which we evaluated using our RaDR-GFP mouse model4,7,43. Fresh liver tissue was imaged for levels of RaDR foci, indicative of recombinant mutant cells, at multiple timepoints up to 10-11 months

post-exposure (Fig. 4d). Strikingly, age had a profound inﬂuence on NDMA-induced large-scale mutations, with juvenile mice displaying a signiﬁcant increase in RaDR foci across all timepoints, peaking at 3 months post-exposure (Fig. 4e). The decline in RaDR foci from 3 to 10 months likely reﬂects turnover of mutant cells or expansion of RaDR-positive regions. Even at 5 ppb NDMA, a small but signiﬁcant increase in RaDR foci was detected at 10 days post exposure in juvenile mice (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In contrast, adult mice displayed only a modest increase in recombination events, ﬁrst detectable at 3 months post-exposure and slightly elevated in longterm mice at 10-11 months post-exposure (Fig. 4e), potentially due to persistent low-level proliferation. The age-dependent discrepancy in NDMA-induced RaDR foci was also evident after intraperitoneal injection, with juveniles displaying an 11-fold increase compared to adults (Supplementary Fig. 1d), further reinforcing the heightened susceptibility of younger animals to NDMA-driven large-scale genomic alterations. Clonal expansion of mutant cells is a crucial step in tumorigenesis, where cells acquiring oncogenic mutations gain a selective advantage and proliferate44. This process allows the mutant cells to accumulate additional genetic and epigenetic alterations, ultimately contributing to the development and progression of cancer. We analyzed liver images from each timepoint for large RaDR foci representative of clonal expansion events8,45. Analysis of long-term mice at 10-11 months post exposure revealed a 5-fold increase in clonal expansion events in juveniles treated with NDMA compared to controls (Fig. 4f), an effect not observed in adults. The substantial increase in de novo mutagenesis and clonal expansion are consistent with early stages of tumor development. Duplex sequencing across a small fraction of the genome (48 kb of 20 endogenous genic and intergenic loci) provided a highly sensitive, quantitative mutagenicity readout and revealed pronounced, agedependent differences in NDMA-induced mutagenesis. Juvenile mice exhibited a dramatic ~186-fold increase in per-base mutation frequency (MFmin) compared to controls (Fig. 4g), while adults showed substantially lower levels (~51-fold, ~3.6-fold less than juveniles), reﬂecting the combined amplifying effects of juvenile proliferation and DNA repair deﬁciency2,6,46,47. NDMA-induced mutation spectra were dominated by GC →AT substitutions, with greater elevation in juveniles (Fig. 4h), and the overall signature primarily matched alkylation-associated COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer) SBS11 (Fig. 4i), conﬁrmed by high similarity to reconstructed proﬁles (Supplementary Fig. 5)6. Duplex sequencing also deﬁned clonal expansion quantitatively by calculating the ratio of MFmax (total mutations) to MFmin (unique mutations), which was markedly increased only in NDMA-treated juveniles (Fig. 4g), directly demonstrating clonal outgrowth of mutant hepatocytes. These mutational ﬁndings are consistent with the observed heightened gptΔ point mutations and clonal expansion of RaDR foci. The concordance across these methods emphasizes the mutational burden in juveniles, providing a mechanistic bridge between early mutagenesis and the later development of liver pathology and tumorigenesis after NDMA exposure.

Exposure age determines severity of liver pathology and cancer risk Results thus far demonstrate that DNA damage, inﬂammation, proliferation, and mutagenesis are more prominent in younger mice exposed to NDMA. For several endpoints, juvenile mice exhibited acute susceptibility, whereas adults appeared completely resistant. To investigate the long-term consequences of NDMA, we evaluated liver pathology 10-11 months post-exposure in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice (Fig. 5a). Younger mice displayed signiﬁcant increases in hepatocellular hypertrophy, hyperplasia, and single-cell necrosis, all features less

pronounced in adults (Fig. 5b)14–16,24,48. Sustained inﬂammation, characterized by persistent immune cell inﬁltration, was observed exclusively in juvenile mice exposed to NDMA. These histopathological changes reﬂectpersistent, low-grade hepaticinﬂammation and cellular stress, accompanied by recurrent cycles of cell death and regeneration, processes known to drive liver cancer development14–16,49. In addition to local tissue damage, NDMA-induced hepatic pathology in juveniles manifested systemically. decrease in long-term body weight compared to controls (Fig. 5c). Notably, this weight loss developed later in life rather than acutely, likely reﬂecting progressive hepatic pathology rather than acute NDMA toxicity (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Consistent with hepatocellular hypertrophy, liver weight was signiﬁcantly increased only in NDMAtreated juvenile mice (Fig. 5c)50. In addition, lung weight was elevated in these animals, in line with the known metabolism of NDMA in pulmonary tissues (Supplementary Fig. 3d)2. Adult mice, however, did not display signiﬁcant changes in body or organ weights. The pronounced separation of these phenotypes between age groups likely underlies differences in cancer susceptibility. Pathological assessment revealed NDMA-treated juvenile mice harbored a signiﬁcantly higher incidence of tumors compared to both untreated controls and adults (Fig. 5d), with neoplasms identiﬁed in the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes (Supplementary Table 1). Liver tumors, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma, were most prevalent in younger mice exposed to NDMA, while none were observed in adults. The severity of liver tumorigenesis in juveniles is further illustrated by representative liver images and histopathology (Fig. 5e, f). Juvenile mice also displayed the highest frequency of NDMA-induced pulmonary adenomas (Supplementary Table 1). Remarkably, submandibular lymphoma was detected exclusively in NDMA-treated juveniles, representing a unique ﬁnding in this study2. Male mice exhibited a higher induction of NDMA-induced γH2AX compared to females (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b), despite equivalent levels of O6MeG and 3MeA DNA adducts (Supplementary Fig. 6c). As expected with hepatic injury, males showed a pronounced induction of proliferation markers (Ki67, PCNA, MCM2; Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Conversely, females demonstrated a more robust p21 (Cdkn1a) induction, as measured via RNA-seq (Fig. 6a) and immunoblotting (Fig. 6b), indicating enhanced cell cycle arrest. Consistent with their strong p21 induction, females did not upregulate proliferation markers following NDMA exposure (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b), reinforcing their reliance on cell cycle arrest over regenerative proliferation and potentially mitigating genotoxic stress. Sex markedly inﬂuenced NDMA’s carcinogenic potential in juvenile mice. Male mice exhibited elevated large-scale mutation (RaDR foci) burdens compared to females at all timepoints up to 10-11 months post-exposure, culminating in a 2-fold difference in long-term mutants (Fig. 6c). This sex disparity extended to the expansion of mutant cells, with clonal expansion events demonstrated only in males (Fig. 6d). Interestingly, point mutations were not signiﬁcantly altered by sex at 3 months post-exposure (Supplementary Fig. 6d). Pathological analysis

aligned with RaDR data, showing that males developed more NDMAinduced hepatocellular hyperplasia (Fig. 6e) and sustained greater weight loss than females (Fig. 6f). These ﬁndings underscore sex as a critical variable in NDMA risk assessment, with male predisposition linked to enhanced and more persistent liver pathologies.

Repair-proﬁcient mice display attenuated juvenile susceptibility While repair-deﬁcient Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice serve as a highly sensitive model, studies in WT mice revealed attenuated but mechanistically similar responses, highlighting both the relevance of NDMA exposure to the general population and the protective effects of functional repair pathways. As expected, the levels of NDMA-induced O6MeG and 3MeA in WT mice were greatly reduced compared to repair-deﬁcient counterparts (Fig. 7a vs. Fig. 1f). Nevertheless, unrepaired O6MeG adducts were signiﬁcantly elevated in both juvenile and adult WT mice, with levels comparable across age groups. Despite low adduct burdens, WT juveniles displayed a statistically signiﬁcant increase in γH2AX suggestive of residual replication stress and DSBs, an effect absent in adults (Fig. 7b, c). Transitioning to downstream effects, WT mice demonstrated mild transcriptomic changes in response to NDMA treatment; however, these changes closely resembled those in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice, including upregulation of Mbl2 (inﬂammation) and Ephx1 (detoxiﬁcation), as well as a juvenile‑speciﬁc downregulation of Cyp2e1 (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b). Indeed, RaDR foci were signiﬁcantly elevated in WT juveniles across all timepoints (Fig. 7e) but resolved faster than in repair-deﬁcient mice (Fig. 4e), with no clonal expansion events detected (Supplementary Fig. 7c). This demonstrates that WT levels of AAG and MGMT proteins limit mutant cell outgrowth despite initial mutation induction. In stark contrast to juveniles, WT adult mice showed no increase in NDMA-induced proliferation (Fig. 7d) or RaDR foci (Fig. 7e), further substantiating the role of age in mutagenic susceptibility. Long-term analysis revealed no histopathological changes in WT mice at 10-11 months post NDMA exposure (Supplementary Fig. 7d). Although NDMA-induced tumors were detected in long-term WT juveniles, the increase was not statistically signiﬁcant compared to adults, which exhibited no tumors (Supplementary Table 1). As expected, detecting subtle NDMA effects in WT mice requires larger cohorts compared to repair-deﬁcient models, reinforcing the utility of Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice for mechanistic studies. Collectively, these results demonstrate that NDMA inﬂicts measurable genomic stress, even in repair competent systems, so long as animals are young.

Discussion While prior studies have investigated the effects of NDMA on young animals, our study provides the ﬁrst in-depth, direct comparison with adults, thereby revealing the biological consequences of NDMA at an early stage of life2. The striking age-dependent differences in response to NDMA exposure highlight a synergistic interaction between developmental stage and environmental exposure. Juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-

mice, deﬁcient in the removal of NDMA-induced 3MeA and O6MeG, displayed markedly elevated levels of downstream DNA damage, inﬂammation, mutagenesis, and liver injury compared to their adult counterparts. These ﬁndings demonstrate the importance of age as a key factor when evaluating the toxicological impact of environmental contaminants, particularly nitrosamines. The dramatic differences between juvenile and adult responses challenge the adequacy of standard adult-centric toxicology testing. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Test Guideline 488 for mutagenicity evaluationpermits the use of younger animals(4-6 weeks old atthe start of treatment) for somatic tissue assessments when scientiﬁcally justiﬁed52. Our data provide clear scientiﬁc justiﬁcation: even in DNA repair-deﬁcient adults exposed to NDMA, downstream effects were substantially attenuated compared to juveniles, despite comparable DNA adduct levels across age groups in both WT and Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice. This clearly demonstrates that juveniles and adults differ fundamentally in their responses to DNA adducts, rather than in adduct formation or removal2,4,7. Given the pronounced differences between juvenile and adult outcomes extending beyond mutations to clonal expansion and tissue

pathology, our ﬁndings from mice younger than the standard guideline recommendations (3 weeks old at the start of treatment) suggest that even earlier exposure windows warrant investigation, and that standard uncertainty factors may underestimate risk for children exposed to NDMA and related nitrosamines53. To directly test the role of proliferation in NDMA susceptibility, we treated adult mice with T3 thyroid hormone, a known inducer of hepatocyte proliferation51. T3 treatment signiﬁcantly increased NDMAinduced γH2AX levels and γH2AX-Ki67 colocalization, demonstrating elevated genotoxicity in dividing cells. Furthermore, T3 exposure ampliﬁed the frequency of sequence rearrangement mutations in NDMA-treated adults, recapitulating juvenile vulnerability. The data support a replication-dependent model, wherein replication forks encountering DNA adducts generate genomic gaps and strand breaks. Therefore, the enhanced susceptibility of juvenile mice stems largely from their elevated hepatocyte proliferation rates, as compared to a disparity originating from traditional toxicokinetic or toxicodynamic differences. This proliferative state exacerbates mutagenesis through replication-driven mutation incorporation and hyperrecombination, effects further ampliﬁed by injury-induced regenerative responses unique to the juvenile liver4–7,14,43. While previous in vivo studies have demonstrated that adult rodents can be susceptible to NDMA-induced mutagenesis, substantial variability remains due to differences in study design and animal models2,9,46,54. In the present work, stringent multiple comparison corrections limited the number of endpoints reaching statistical signiﬁcance in adults. By prioritizing a conservative statistical analysis approach, the reliability of conclusions is strengthened, emphasizing that age is a key determinant of NDMA susceptibility. For these studies, we focused primarily on DNA repair-deﬁcient animals exposed to a relatively high dose of NDMA to minimize animal use while maximizing detection sensitivity. Although this approach limits direct environmental relevance, both MGMT and AAG exhibit wide interindividual variability, including naturally occurring variants with reduced repair capacity documented in human cancers, highlighting the importance of genetic diversity in toxicological studies and supporting the Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- model as a physiologically relevant system2,4,7. Comparable biological responses were observed in DNA repair-deﬁcient juveniles following both drinking water and intraperitoneal NDMA administration, showing that the route of exposure does not markedly inﬂuence hepatic outcomes. Even at a much lower, more environmentally relevant dose, we still detected a cellular stress response, demonstrating the heightened sensitivity of younger animals. In repair-proﬁcient WT mice, juveniles also exhibited NDMAinduced DNA damage, proliferation, and large-scale mutations, though at reduced levels, emphasizing the need for expanded WT studies with larger cohorts. DNA adduct analysis DNA was isolated from 100 mg of frozen liver tissue using the Qiagen 100/G genomic tip following the procedure recommended for genomic DNA preparation. Brieﬂy, liver tissue was homogenized in buffer QBT in the presence of RNase and proteinase K and incubated overnight at room temperature. The solution was loaded onto a Qiagen 100/G tip, washed with buffer QC, and retained DNA was eluted with buffer QF. DNA was precipitated with isopropanol and recovered by spooling onto a glass rod which was washed with 70% ethanol, brieﬂy dried and then dissolved in 500 µL of puriﬁed water. The amount of recovered DNA was determined via UV absorption using a NanoDrop One C spectrometer (Thermo Scientiﬁc). DNA (100-125 µg) containing 10 µg of methylated 15N E. coli DNA, which served as an internal standard, was hydrolyzed by addition of 50 µL formic acid and heating at 95 oC for 1 h. Hydrolyzed DNA samples containing isotopically labeled standards were loaded onto Strata X SC cartridges (100 mg; Phenomenex), which had been prewashed with acetonitrile followed by water. The cartridges were then washed with 15 mL of 0.1 N hydrochloric acid. The retained compounds were eluted with a solution containing 1.5 mL 5% ammonium hydroxide, 10% EtOH, H2O, and vacuum centrifuged to dryness at room temperature. Samples were reconstituted in 100 µL of 0.1 N HCl and transferred to glass vials for LC/QQQ MS analysis. LC/ESI-MS/MS analysis was performed on an Agilent 6410 Triple Quadrupole Mass Spectrometer interfaced with an Agilent 1100 series HPLC. Samples (25 µL injected) were resolved on a 4.6 × 150 mm, 3.5 µm Eclipse Plus C18 column (Agilent Technologies) eluted at a ﬂow rate of 0.5 mL/min. The column was eluted with a step gradient of 4 mM ammonium acetate containing 2% acetonitrile (solvent A) to 100% acetonitrile/0.0001% acetic acid (solvent B) over a period of 30 min followed by column re-equilibration. QQQ MS analysis was performed in the positive ion mode using N2 as the nebulizing/drying gas. Capillary voltage was 4.0 kV, and the temperature was set at 350 °C. Selective reaction monitoring (SRM) was used for quantitative analysis of methylated purines with the collision energy set at 25 for methylated guanines and 30 for the methylated adenine. Nitrogen was used as the collision gas. The following transitions were monitored: m/z 166 [M + H]+ →m/z 149 for O6MeG; m/z 171 [M + H]+ →m/z 153 for O6-methyl-15N-guanine; m/z 150 [M + H]+ →m/z 108 for 3MeA; and m/z 155 [M + H]+ →m/z 112 for 3-methyl-15N-adenine.

RNAseq Total RNA was extracted from ≤30 mg mouse liver tissue stored in RNAlater at −20 °C using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen, #74134). Following the template switching reaction, cDNA from 24 wells containing unique well identiﬁers were pooled together and cleaned using RNA Ampure beads at 1.0X. cDNA was eluted with 17 µL of water, followed by digestion with Exonuclease I at 37 °C for 30 min, and inactivated at 80 °C for 20 min. Differential expression was assessed using the two-sided Wald test in DESeq2 (v1.49.1), and log2 fold-change estimates were calculated using lfcShrink with the apeglm method65,66. Volcano plots were constructed to display -log10 p-values versus log2 fold changes, highlighting genes with raw p < 0.05 and |log2 fold change | > 0.58. RaDR Immediately after excision, the left liver lobe was preserved in PBS containing 0.01% trypsin inhibitor on ice. The tissue was placed between a glass slide and coverslip, then imaged using a Nikon Eclipse Ti2 microscope (2x objective) with an Andor Zyla VSC-03269 camera using NIS-Elements AR software (v5.11.02). One-channel images (FITC: EGFP) were captured under identical exposure settings across samples. RaDR foci (EGFP positive cells) were identiﬁed and quantiﬁed using a custom two-stage machine learning algorithm5. This algorithm integrates intensity and gradient-based pipelines with a pre-trained support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish true foci from noise, enhancing detection accuracy for both shallow and deep tissue events. Foci counts were normalized to the visible liver area in each image. For clonal expansion analysis, a custom ImageJ (v1.54p) macro was used to quantify the size of ﬂuorescent foci. Images were processed with Gaussian blur, thresholding, and watershed segmentation to deﬁne regions of interest. Foci exceeding 2000 pixels were classiﬁed as clonal expansion events based on visual conﬁrmation. The number of clonal expansion events per liver lobe was quantiﬁed.

Duplex sequencing Liver genomic DNA was analyzed by targeted duplex sequencing to quantify mutation frequency and characterize mutation spectra47. Genomic DNA was isolated from ~20 mg of liver tissue using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, #69504). DNA concentration was measured with the Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc, #Q33266), and DNA integrity was assessed on a TapeStation using Genomic DNA ScreenTape (Agilent, #5067-5365/5067-5366). Samples with a DNA integrity number (DIN) > 7 were selected for library preparation. Libraries were prepared for duplex sequencing using the Mouse MutagenesisPanel v2.0 (TwinStrand Biosciences). The panel targets 20 genomic regions (~48 kb total) distributed across the mouse autosomes and is designed to approximate genome-wide diversity in sequence context, GC content, chromatin state, and coding status47. For each sample, 500 ng of genomic DNA was enzymatically fragmented, end-polished, A-tailed, and ligated to duplex sequencing adapters with unique molecular identiﬁers. Final libraries were quantiﬁed with the Qubit dsDNA High Sensitivity Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc, #Q33231), and average fragment size was assessed on a TapeStation using High Sensitivity D1000 ScreenTape (Agilent, #5067- 5584/5067-5585). Libraries were pooled and submitted to Psomagen (Rockville, MD) for sequencing. Libraries were sequenced on two lanes of a NovaSeq X 25B ﬂow cell (Illumina, #20104706), targeting ~400 million reads passing-ﬁlter per sample and at least 10,000-fold target locus coverage. Sequencing yielded a mean of ~489 million passing-ﬁlter reads per sample, a mean on-target duplex depth >15,000x, and a mean peak tag-family size of 31. FASTQ ﬁles were processed with the TwinStrand duplex sequencing Mutagenesis App v4.6.1 (TwinStrand Biosciences) to generate persite mutation calls. Mutation ﬁles were then imported into R and summarized with MutSeqR to calculate mutation frequencies (MF).

Variant calls were ﬁltered using a variant allele frequency (VAF) threshold of 0.01 to remove likely mosaic or germline variants, and single-nucleotide variants overlapping germline multinucleotide variants were excluded. We computed MF under two assumptions: MFmin, which collapses identical within-sample mutations to a single event, and MFmax, which counts all mutations, including identical occurrences. Model adequacy was evaluated, and no overdispersion was detected. Adjusted means and contrasts were obtained with emmeans70. Statistics and reproducibility An equal number of male and female mice from each cohort were used for analysis. For endpoints with excess mice of one sex, individuals were randomly excluded from analysis to balance group sizes using a cryptographically secure random number generator. Mice from separate litters were included to the maximum extent for heterogeneity. Due to lack of litter and cage treatment variability as demonstrated by the sensitive RaDR mutational assay (Supplementary Fig. 10d), each mouse represents a biological replicate (n = 1), and all measurements were obtained from independent samples. Data analysis and graph generation were performed using GraphPad Prism (v10.4.2). Statistical analyses included two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple comparison test, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparison test, unpaired two-sided t-test, two-sided chi-squared test, and generalized linear mixed model as appropriate. Normality was evaluated using the Shapiro-Wilk test prior to applying parametric tests and statistical signiﬁcance was deﬁned as p < 0.05 (adjusted for multiple comparisons where applicable). Details regarding the speciﬁc statistical analyses, treatment timepoints, exact signiﬁcant p-values, and sample sizes (n) are described in the ﬁgures and legends, with individual biological replicates displayed as discrete data points where applicable.
